title: Nouns & Pronouns
subtitle: The Village of Many Names
intro: Names multiply, own things, and wear different masks depending on their job. In this village you will learn plurals, possession, and how to pick the right pronoun every time.

rules.title: Regular Plurals
rules.tagline: Add -s, -es or -ies to make more than one

story.line: A merchant's stall is piled with goods. Hana must write the price list.
One fox, two foxs? That looks wrong.
Say it aloud. Fox-es. When a word ends in a hissing sound (s, x, z, ch, sh), English adds a little extra syllable: -es.
And one berry, two berrys? Hehe.
Consonant plus y? The y turns into i and adds -es: berries. But a vowel plus y just adds -s: keys, days.
So: cats, foxes, berries, keys. The price list is done!

parts.name: Most nouns: add -s
parts.detail: The default rule.

parts.name: Hissing endings: add -es
parts.detail: Words ending in s, ss, x, z, ch, sh.

parts.name: Consonant + y: change to -ies
parts.detail: If a consonant comes before y.

parts.name: Vowel + y: just add -s
parts.detail: If a vowel comes before y.

parts.name: Some -f / -fe: change to -ves
parts.detail: Old words that softened their sound.

rules.history:
In Old English there were several ways to make plurals. One group of nouns used the ending -as: stān (stone) became stānas. After the Norman Conquest, this -as ending (which became -es and then -s) slowly took over almost all nouns, because it was the easiest pattern to remember.

The -es with an extra syllable survives after hissing sounds simply because 'foxs' is nearly impossible to say clearly.

examples.note: Consonant + y → ies, vowel + y → s.

rules.trick: If saying the plural makes you hiss twice (fox-es, wish-es), you need -es.

quiz.why: Dish ends in sh, so add -es.
A vowel (e) comes before y, so just add -s.

rules.title: Irregular Plurals
rules.tagline: The rebels: men, feet, mice, children

story.line: I defeated two mouses and three gooses!
Pfft! Mice and geese, warrior.
Why don't they follow the -s rule?!
They are ancient rebels, older than the -s rule's victory. Long ago, a vowel inside the word changed instead: mouse, mice. Goose, geese. Foot, feet.
And some never change at all, like sheep and deer?
Exactly. One sheep, a hundred sheep. You must simply learn the rebels by heart.

parts.name: Vowel change
parts.detail: man → men, woman → women, foot → feet, tooth → teeth, goose → geese, mouse → mice.
parts.example: My feet hurt after the march.

parts.name: -en plurals
parts.detail: child → children, ox → oxen.

parts.name: No change
parts.detail: sheep, deer, fish, series, species.

parts.name: Latin and Greek words
parts.detail: cactus → cacti, crisis → crises, phenomenon → phenomena.

rules.history:
Vowel-change plurals come from a sound change called i-mutation that happened in early Germanic languages, over 1,300 years ago. An old plural ending with an 'i' sound pulled the vowel of the word forward, and later the ending itself disappeared, leaving only the changed vowel. German still does this: Fuß, Füße.

Children and oxen keep an old -en plural ending. Children is actually a double plural: Old English cildru plus an extra -en.

examples.good: Two women and three children arrived.
examples.bad: Two womans and three childs arrived.

rules.trick: Rebel chant: 'One mouse in the house, two mice on the ice. One goose on the loose, two geese in the trees.'

quiz.why: Deer stays the same in the plural.

rules.title: Possessive Nouns
rules.tagline: Use 's to show who owns what

story.line: A sword lies in the grass. Everyone claims it.
That's Kaitos sword!
Without the apostrophe, it looks like there are many Kaitos. Write Kaito's: apostrophe then s.
What if two students own the same dojo?
The plural already ends in s, so just add the apostrophe after it: the students' dojo.
And the children's toys? Children has no s!
Then add 's as usual: children's.

parts.name: Singular noun: add 's
parts.detail: Even if it ends in s, most style guides add 's.

parts.name: Plural ending in s: add '
parts.detail: Only the apostrophe.

parts.name: Plural not ending in s: add 's
parts.detail: Irregular plurals.
parts.example: the women's team, the mice's nest

parts.name: Joint ownership
parts.detail: Only the last name gets 's when they share one thing.

rules.history:
In Old English, a noun showed ownership with an ending, often -es: 'cynges' meant 'king's.' Over time the e vanished from both speech and writing.

In the 1500s and 1600s, printers began using an apostrophe to mark the missing letter. Some scholars even believed (wrongly) that 'the king's crown' was short for 'the king his crown.' The apostrophe stuck, and for plurals it moved after the s in the 1700s.

examples.note: Many players, so the apostrophe goes after the s.
Men is already plural, so add 's.

rules.trick: Write the owner first, complete (dragon, players, men). Then add the apostrophe. If it doesn't end in s, add an s too.

quiz.why: Plural ending in s: add only the apostrophe.

rules.title: Countable vs. Uncountable
rules.tagline: Some things you count, some you measure

story.line: Innkeeper! Bring me three rices and two waters!
Hahaha! Do you want him to count every grain?
Rice and water are uncountable. They come as a mass, so you measure them: three bowls of rice, two glasses of water.
But onigiri are countable. Three onigiri, please!
Correct. Countable nouns take a, an, many, few. Uncountable nouns take much, little, some, and never a or an.

parts.name: Countable nouns
parts.detail: Have singular and plural forms. Use a/an, many, few, a number.

parts.name: Uncountable nouns
parts.detail: No plural form. Liquids, materials, ideas, and some collective things.

parts.name: Measure words
parts.detail: Make uncountable nouns countable.
parts.example: a piece of advice, two cups of tea

parts.name: Both!
parts.detail: Some nouns switch meaning: 'a light' (a lamp) vs. 'light' (brightness).
parts.example: Two coffees, please. (cups) / I love coffee. (the drink)

rules.history:
English didn't decide this randomly. Nouns that name a substance or a mass without clear edges, like sand, water or gold, have always behaved as a single blob of stuff.

Some surprises, like information, advice and furniture, came from French and Latin as mass words. Other languages count them freely (French says 'des informations'), which is why learners often write 'informations.' In English, they stayed uncountable.

examples.good: Can you give me some advice?
examples.bad: Can you give me an advice?

examples.good: She gave me three pieces of information.
examples.note: Use a measure word to count.

rules.trick: Ask: can I put a number right in front of it? 'Three cookies' works, 'three rices' doesn't. No number? Uncountable.

quiz.why: Money is uncountable, so use much.
Luggage is uncountable: a piece of luggage.

rules.title: I or Me? He or Him?
rules.tagline: Subject pronouns act, object pronouns receive

story.line: Me and Hana defeated the boss!
Remove Hana. Would you say 'Me defeated the boss'?
No... 'I defeated the boss.' So it's 'Hana and I defeated the boss'!
Then the boss gave a reward to Hana and I!
Remove Hana again. 'The boss gave a reward to I'?
Ugh. 'To me.' So: 'to Hana and me.' You win this time, owl.

parts.name: Subject pronouns
parts.detail: Do the action: I, you, he, she, it, we, they.

parts.name: Object pronouns
parts.detail: Receive the action or follow a preposition: me, you, him, her, it, us, them.

parts.name: The remove test
parts.detail: Take away the other person and see which pronoun sounds right.
parts.example: (Hana and) I went. / for (Hana and) me

parts.name: Politeness order
parts.detail: Put yourself last.
parts.example: Kaito and I, not I and Kaito.

rules.history:
Old English nouns and pronouns all changed form depending on whether they were the subject or the object. Over the centuries, nouns lost these changes, but pronouns held on: I/me, he/him, we/us, they/them.

That's why only pronouns cause this headache. 'Hana and I' feels fancy to some people, so they overuse it even after prepositions. Grammar teachers call this hypercorrection.

examples.good: Hana and I went to the festival.
examples.bad: Me and Hana went to the festival.

examples.note: After a preposition, use object pronouns.

rules.trick: Cover up the other person with your thumb. Whatever sounds right alone is right in the pair.

quiz.q: 'The teacher gave the scrolls to Kaito and ___.'
quiz.why: Remove Kaito: 'gave the scrolls to me.'

rules.title: Who vs. Whom
rules.tagline: Who is like he, whom is like him

story.line: A secret letter arrives. It is addressed: 'To who it may concern.'
This letter is a fake. A true scholar would never write 'to who.'
How can you tell so fast?
Use the HE/HIM test. Answer the question with he or him. 'It may concern him.' Him has an M, so you need whoM.
And 'Who stole the scroll?' becomes 'He stole the scroll.' No M, so who!

parts.name: Who = subject
parts.detail: Does the action, like he/she/they.

parts.name: Whom = object
parts.detail: Receives the action or follows a preposition, like him/her/them.
parts.example: Whom did you call? (I called him.)

parts.name: After prepositions
parts.detail: To whom, for whom, with whom.
parts.example: For whom does the bell toll?

parts.name: Everyday speech
parts.detail: In casual talk, most people use who everywhere. Whom is for careful writing.

rules.history:
Who and whom come from Old English hwā and hwām. Hwām was the form used after prepositions and for objects, just like him and them, which share that same old -m ending.

Whom has been fading from everyday speech for hundreds of years. Linguists expect it may eventually survive only in fixed phrases like 'to whom it may concern.'

examples.note: Formal writing: the dragon chose him, so whom.

examples.good: Who is knocking at the gate?
examples.bad: Whom is knocking at the gate?

examples.good: To whom should I give this?
examples.bad: To who should I give this?

rules.trick: him = whom. Both end in M.

quiz.why: You travel with him, so whom.

rules.title: Pronoun Agreement
rules.tagline: A pronoun must match the noun it replaces

story.line: The dojo notice board reads: 'Every student must bring his or her own sword.'
That's long. Can we say 'their own sword'?
Yes. Singular they, for a person whose gender is unknown or not important, has been used for more than 600 years.
But then there's this one: 'The team lost their way.' And 'The team lost its way.'
Both are seen. American English usually treats a team as one unit, so it. British English often uses they for the members. Just stay consistent.

parts.name: Number
parts.detail: Singular nouns get singular pronouns; plural nouns get plural pronouns.

parts.name: Person
parts.detail: Don't switch from 'one' or 'a person' to 'you' midway.
parts.example: If a person trains, they improve.

parts.name: Singular they
parts.detail: For an unknown person or someone who uses they.

parts.name: Clear antecedent
parts.detail: The reader must know which noun the pronoun means.
parts.example: Hana told Yumi that Yumi was late.

rules.history:
Singular they appears in writing at least as far back as the 1300s, and writers like Chaucer, Shakespeare and Jane Austen used it.

In the 1700s some grammar writers decided 'he' should be the default for everyone. That rule was a fashion of its time. Today major style guides, including the Chicago Manual of Style and the AP Stylebook, accept singular they.

examples.good: Each player has their own locker.
When Hana met Yumi, Hana smiled.
examples.bad: When Hana met Yumi, she smiled.
examples.note: The second is unclear: who smiled?

rules.trick: Point at the pronoun and ask: who exactly are you? If the answer is fuzzy or doesn't match in number, fix it.

options: Kaito told Ren he was late.
quiz.why: Who was late: Kaito or Ren?
